So I actually looked in the continuance for the three dates. There was trials going on in that same courtroom for those dates. Now, and this also goes to the point where Justice Merriman had made earlier. The trial court actually technically did rule on the suppression issue. So again, going back to the waiver, the people's position is that the appellate review is precluded because when you do not comply with the timeliness requirements, you are precluded from taking that up on appeal. And the Seventh Circuit has made very clear, analogizing, because this is based on Rule 12B, it's the analogous rule to the RR statute, 8GCA 65.45. Exceptions for timeliness are the exceptions, it's an exception to the rule and should not be, the relief from the waiver should not be granted because the timeliness requirements. Now, I also want to add that the trial court did also say that the time standards was what was keeping him confined to the motion deadline, but he still did find, issued a decision order on that matter. The people submitted there is reasonable suspicion for this traffic stop based on even the anonymous tip alone. While this court has made clear in emancipate that if the anonymous tip has an indicia of reliability where there is a crime being alleged and there's sufficient information given by the anonymous tipster that would indicate that this is reliable warranting a stop, then the traffic stop, any police officer would have reasonable suspicion. In this case, the tip was specifically that the driver of this make and model of a car was drunk driving. Now, it is important to note that the officer didn't even stop the defendant at that point. He did activate his sirens, but the defendant did not comply. And then the officer observed him run a red light. The court has also held that when a police officer observes any type of violation of a crime or traffic violation, that is also reasonable suspicion for a stop. So we have the two reasonable suspicion based on two different things. One is the tipster's personal observations and the other one is the police officer's personal observations. And the United States Supreme Court has said this is sufficient. When you look at the anonymous tipster's personal observation, specificity of the vehicle, contemporaneous reporting and the use of 911 phone calls alleging a criminal activity, then that would give an officer reasonable suspicion for the stop. So I actually think that the rule is that the officer wouldn't have even needed to observe for himself the disobeying the red light. There was already reasonable suspicion based on the anonymous tip. And so it is under People v. Johnson and here's why. In People v. Emancipate, this court overturned the conviction based on the stop or upheld the suppression because all the anonymous tipster did was say, there is a person with weapons. This is again, different from that because we have the reliability of the tip, which is what is distinguished. So under the Plain Error Standard Review, the people submit that this conviction for DUI as a misdemeanor should be affirmed because there was no violation of any Fourth Amendment right of the defendant appellant.
